sections.normalized_html:
Recall that if [MATH: X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}] are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function [MATH: f(x; \theta),] where [MATH: \theta] is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample [MATH: x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n] is

[MATH: l(θ)|= \ln L(θ); = \ln (∏_(i = 1)^(n)f(x_{i}; θ)); = ∑_(i = 1)^(n)\ln (f(x_{i}; θ)).]

We are given a sample of [MATH: n=10] independent Bernoulli random variables with unknown parameter [MATH: \theta.] Therefore, the probability mass function is

[MATH: f(x;\theta) = \theta^x(1-\theta)^{1-x}, \qquad x=0, 1.]

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

[MATH: l(θ)|= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)\ln (θ^{x_{i}}(1 − θ)^{1 − x_{i}}); = ∑_(i = 1)^(n)\ln (θ^{x_{i}}) + \ln ((1 − θ)^{1 − x_{i}}); = ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i}\ln θ + (1 − x_{i})\ln (1 − θ); = \ln θ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i} + \ln (1 − θ)∑_(i = 1)^(n)(1 − x_{i}); = S\ln θ + (n − S)\ln (1 − θ)]

where [MATH: \displaystyle S = \sum_ {i=1}^n x_i] is the number of successes in the sample.

Finally, since there are [MATH: 7] successes in the sample, we have

[MATH: l(θ)|= 7\ln θ + (10 − 7)\ln (1 − θ); = 7\ln θ + 3\ln (1 − θ).]

[MATH: x_1 = 4, \qquad x_2 = 1, \qquad x_3 = 1.]
Find the log-likelihood function of this sample.

Hint: The probability mass function for a binomial random variable is given by
[MATH: f(x) = \displaystyle \binom{5}{x} \theta^x (1-\theta)^{5-x}, \qquad x = 0,1, \ldots, 5.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that if [MATH: X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}] are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function [MATH: f(x; \theta),] where [MATH: \theta] is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample [MATH: x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n] is [MATH: l(θ)|= \ln L(θ); = \ln (∏_(i = 1)^(n)f(x_{i}, θ)); = ∑_(i = 1)^(n)\ln (f(x_{i}, θ)).]

In our case, we are given a sample of [MATH: n = 3] independent binomial random variables with an unknown probability of success [MATH: \theta] and [MATH: N = 5] as the number of trials. Therefore, the probability mass function is

[MATH: f(x, θ)|= ((N)/(x))θ^{x}(1 − θ)^{N − x}, x = 0, 1, …, N; = ((5)/(x))θ^{x}(1 − θ)^{5 − x}, x = 0, 1, …, 5.]

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows: [MATH: l(θ)|= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)\ln (((5)/(x_{i}))θ^{x_{i}}(1 − θ)^{5 − x_{i}}); = ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(\ln ((5)/(x_{i})) + \ln (θ^{x_{i}}) + \ln ((1 − θ)^{5 − x_{i}})); = ∑_(i = 1)^(n)\ln ((5)/(x_{i})) + ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i}\ln θ + ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(5 − x_{i})\ln (1 − θ); = ∑_(i = 1)^(n)\ln ((5)/(x_{i})) + \ln θ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i} + \ln (1 − θ)∑_(i = 1)^(n)(5 − x_{i}); = ∑_(i = 1)^(n)\ln ((5)/(x_{i})) + S\ln θ + (5n − S)\ln (1 − θ)] where [MATH: \displaystyle S = \sum_ {i=1}^n x_i.]

Now, note that [MATH: ∑_(i = 1)^(n)\ln ((5)/(x_{i}))|= \ln ((5)/(x_{1})) + \ln ((5)/(x_{2})) + \ln ((5)/(x_{3})); = \ln (∏_(i = 1)^(n)((5)/(x_{i}))).]

So, our expression for [MATH: l(\theta)] becomes [MATH: l(\theta) = \ln\left( \prod_{i=1}^n {5 \choose x_i}\right) + S\ln \theta + (5n - S) \ln(1-\theta).]

Now, using the sample data with [MATH: n=3,] we have [MATH: ∏_(i = 1)^(n)((5)/(x_{i}))|= ((5)/(4)) ⋅ ((5)/(1)) ⋅ ((5)/(1)); = 5 ⋅ 5 ⋅ 5; = 125,]

and [MATH: S = 4 + 1 + 1 = 6.]

Substituting the above values into our expression for [MATH: l(\theta)], we get [MATH: l(θ)|= \ln (125) + 6\ln θ + (5 ⋅ 3 − 6)\ln (1 − θ); = \ln 125 + 6\ln θ + 9\ln (1 − θ).]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Recall that if [MATH: X_1, \: X_2, \: \ldots, \: X_{n}] are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function [MATH: f(x; \theta),] where [MATH: \theta] is an unknown parameter, then the likelihood function of a random sample [MATH: x_1, \: x_2, \: \ldots, \: x_n] is

Content:
[MATH: L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i;\,\theta).]

Content:
For example, if

Content:
[MATH: X_1,\quad X_2,\quad X_3,\quad X_4,\quad X_5,\quad X_6]
is an I.I.D random sample with [MATH: X_i\sim \text{Bernoulli}(\theta),] where [MATH: \theta] is the unknown probability of success, then the likelihood function of the sample

Content:
[MATH: x_1=0, \quad x_2=1, \quad x_3=1, \quad x_4=0, \quad x_5=1, \quad x_6=1]

Content:
is given by

Content:
[MATH: L(\theta) = \theta^{4}(1-\theta)^{2}.]

Content:
The likelihood function contains lots of products, which can be cumbersome to work with. To make things easier, we convert the products into sums by finding the natural logarithm of [MATH: L(\theta),] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: l(θ)|= \ln (L(θ)); = \ln (∏_(i = 1)^(n)f(x_{i}; θ)); = \ln (f(x_{1}; θ) ⋅ f(x_{2}; θ)⋯f(x_{n}; θ)); = \ln (f(x_{1}; θ)) + \ln (f(x_{2}; θ)) + ⋯ + \ln (f(x_{n}; θ)); = ∑_(i = 1)^(n)\ln (f(x_{i}; θ))]

Content:
This new function [MATH: l(\theta)] is called the log-likelihood function of the sample.

Content:
For our Bernoulli example above, the corresponding log-likelihood function is as follows:

Content:
[MATH: l(θ)|= \ln (θ^{4}(1 − θ)^{2}); = \ln (θ^{4}) + \ln ((1 − θ)^{2}); = 4\ln θ + 2\ln (1 − θ)]

---

Item 3 — Example: Log-Likelihood Functions for Bernoulli Random Variables

Example Prompt:
Suppose [MATH: X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_{10}] is an I.I.D random sample where [MATH: X_i\sim \text{Bernoulli}(\theta)] with unknown probability of success [MATH: \theta.] For a particular sample [MATH: x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{10},] you're given that there are [MATH: 7] successes. Find the log-likelihood function of the sample.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that if [MATH: X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}] are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function [MATH: f(x; \theta),] where [MATH: \theta] is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample [MATH: x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n] is

[MATH: l(θ)|= \ln L(θ); = \ln (∏_(i = 1)^(n)f(x_{i}; θ)); = ∑_(i = 1)^(n)\ln (f(x_{i}; θ)).]

We are given a sample of [MATH: n=10] independent Bernoulli random variables with unknown parameter [MATH: \theta.] Therefore, the probability mass function is

[MATH: f(x;\theta) = \theta^x(1-\theta)^{1-x}, \qquad x=0, 1.]

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

[MATH: l(θ)|= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)\ln (θ^{x_{i}}(1 − θ)^{1 − x_{i}}); = ∑_(i = 1)^(n)\ln (θ^{x_{i}}) + \ln ((1 − θ)^{1 − x_{i}}); = ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i}\ln θ + (1 − x_{i})\ln (1 − θ); = \ln θ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i} + \ln (1 − θ)∑_(i = 1)^(n)(1 − x_{i}); = S\ln θ + (n − S)\ln (1 − θ)]

where [MATH: \displaystyle S = \sum_ {i=1}^n x_i] is the number of successes in the sample.

Finally, since there are [MATH: 7] successes in the sample, we have

[MATH: l(θ)|= 7\ln θ + (10 − 7)\ln (1 − θ); = 7\ln θ + 3\ln (1 − θ).]
